newsitem.title: USA: Sprint affiliate frowns on brokers' junk bond ads.
newsitem.headline: Sprint affiliate frowns on brokers' junk bond ads.

text.p: An affiliate of Sprint Corp. plans to ask a New York securities broker to change ads for the affiliate's junk bonds, fearing that references to Sprint Corp.'s national advertising campaign may mislead investors.

A spokesman for the Sprint affiliate, Sprint Spectrum L.P., said Thursday that its legal counsel would ask the securities firm, Kirlin Securities Inc., of Syosset, N.Y., to stop broadcasting the ads, which include references to Sprint's familiar "pin-drop" advertising campaign and its spokeswoman, Candice Bergen.
However, the bonds Kirlin is hawking were not issued by Sprint Corp., the country's third-largest long-distance telephone company.

The bonds actually are unsecured notes issued by Sprint Spectrum, a limited partnership that is 40 percent owned by Sprint. Sprint is not associated with the debt and has no obligation regarding its payment.

"Obviously, they are using some of the messages from Sprint Corp. mixed in with some of the key messages from Sprint Spectrum. We want to be sure that no one is misled," said Ed Mattix a spokesman for Sprint Spectrum.
He said Sprint Spectrum would send Kirlin a "strongly worded" letter asking that the company stop misrepresenting the issuer of the bonds and that it would take further action if necessary.
Sprint Spectrum, which provides digital personal communications services, learned of the Kirlin ads when asked about the campaign by a Reuters reporter.
Kirlin is running the ad on local radio stations urging customers to invest in a "Sprint bond with a yield to maturity of over 9 percent."
The ad borrows a portion of Sprint's advertising slogan, stating: "We think it's as clear as a pin drop that Sprint bonds are for you."
The ad also makes reference to Bergen. "Candice Bergen has already told you how clear Sprint is. Now Kirlin Securities wants to tell you how clear it is for you to invest in Sprint bonds."

A Kirlin sales representative told a telephone caller, "The company is Sprint Corporation ... it's a household name," adding that "Sprint Corporation fully backs it (the bonds). It is their senior debt."

"This is just awful," said Marilyn Cohen, president of Envision Capital Management Inc., referring to the ad. Envision Capital is a Los Angeles-based firm that manages bond investments for retail clients.
"They don't give enough details about these securities in their ads. There is nothing wrong with junk bonds if you are a professional; but they are targeting the retail investor with money here."

Sprint Spectrum bonds are rated "highly speculative," or "single-B," by major credit ratings agencies Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's. These are ratings generally considered "junk" in market parlance.
By comparison, Sprint Corp. bonds are rated several notches higher at "single-A," or "investment grade."
A Sprint Corp. spokesman declined to comment on the matter.
Market experts describe junk bonds as volatile securities that are appropriate only for experienced investors.

"They are called junk for a reason," said Robert Anthony, an attorney with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission here. "It seems to me that an ad should bring out the fact that these securites are not for everyone."
Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc., for instance, prohibits its salespeople from soliciting retail customers directly for junk bond sales because of the risks involved.
The Sprint bonds do not begin paying interest for several years, making them particularly volatile to changes in interest rates.
Robert Gennari, director of marketing at Kirlin and the author of the ad, said the firm chose not to mention Sprint Spectrum because "We didn't want to confuse the listener."

Gennari said the firm did not feel it was necessary to mention in the ad that Sprint Spectrum junk bonds were different than Sprint Corp. bonds. "It's like buying a (Chevrolet) Geo instead of buying a Toyota -- it's the same car but it's just built in a different factory."

Gennari said the ads included a disclaimer that said: "These bonds involve a greater risk than investment grade issues." However, a Kirlin ad run recently over a local New York station omitted that sentence.

Gennari denied any knowledge of a salesperson who was misleading investors about the issuer of the bond. "I can't monitor every single broker that we have ... We certainly have not told the brokers, 'Yeah, sell it as a Sprint Corp. bond' because it's not ... He may be misinformed; he might be a rookie broker, you never know."

Kirlin is a full-service brokerage firm with several offices around the country. The firm has been running the ad since June, and Gennari said Kirlin planned to continue the campaign for the next two weeks.
Kirlin has been the subject of several disciplinary actions in the past several years, according to the National Association of Securities Dealers.
Since 1991, the firm has settled in arbitration with customers three cases involving misrepresentation and suitability of securities, and omission of facts, according to the NASD.
Gennari, who said Kirlin had already sold "a ton" of the bonds, added: "We're not in the business of misleading people. We are a very conservative firm; we look for value in our investments."
